title: Distributed Parallel Structure-Aware Presolving for Arrowhead Linear Programs
contribution: A distributed, structure-preserving presolve and postsolve framework inside the parallel interior-point solver PIPS-IPM++ for arrowhead LPs. On 82 mostly energy-system LPs it is about 6 times faster than Gurobi's presolve and 19 times faster than PaPILO's on one 64-process node, and 20 to 115 times faster than Gurobi's on multiple nodes for large instances with small linking parts, while removing fewer nonzeros. It raises PIPS-IPM++'s solved count from 37 to 48, whereas external presolve with automatic re-annotation lets PIPS-IPM++ solve at most 21.
problem_entry: Presolve for structure-exploiting parallel IPMs is serial and structure-agnostic, can become the bottleneck and can destroy the arrowhead structure the solver needs; general libraries, including the group's own PaPILO, lose the block assignment (pp. 1–3).
key_idea: Classify reductions as local (one block, no communication) or global (linking parts, synchronization points); keep one postsolve stack per process with buffered linking updates; enforce the arrowhead form as an invariant; add a Permutation and a blockwise LinDependencies presolver. The reductions themselves come from the literature (pp. 5–11).
assumptions: Continuous LP (equality and ranged rows, possibly infinite bounds, no integers) in arrowhead form, with the modeller's block annotation read through GAMS; one block per process and the 0-block on every process; 82 instances, almost all energy-system models with nearly equal block sizes, 69 public; full row rank of A0 and of every B_i gives full row rank without the linking rows (pp. 4, 7, 9–10, 12–13).
proof_devices: Structure invariant: no presolver may destroy the arrowhead form or create linking rows or columns, even if it could improve size or stability (p. 7)
Local and global reduction classes, with global reductions as synchronization points and one postsolve stack per process (pp. 7–8)
Buffered linking quantities, with synchronization events recorded on the stack and replayed in postsolve (pp. 10–11)
Blockwise rank argument and MA50-like elimination on [B_i I] with pivots restricted to the block's columns; dependencies through linking rows left to the Schur-complement factorization (pp. 9–10)

Permutation presolver without fixed-point iteration (columns before rows, detect all candidates, then move); 0-link variables as sparse, communication-free Schur-complement blocks, Eq. (6) (pp. 8–9, 21)
Two-level hashing with a custom-operator Allreduce of support hashes and an AND-Allreduce of per-process parallelism flags, Algorithms 1–2 (pp. 11–12, 24–26)
Deterministic MPI collectives through Intel MPI's conditional numerical reproducibility, I_MPI_CBWR=2 (p. 13)

Scaling explained by Amdahl's sequential fraction, Spearman correlations with structure, and a decomposition of communication into collectives × cost per collective plus local work (pp. 14, 17, 26–27)
experiments: Setup: 82 LPs (69 public with scripts and logs), LRZ terrabyte full nodes, PaPILO 3.0.1, Gurobi 13.0.0, PIPS-IPM++ d34cee38, SGM shifts 1 s and 1%, single deterministic runs. Scaling on 8 large instances chosen by a written rule: 30–50× at 64 processes, sequential fraction 0.4–1.8%; only 23× and 7× with large linking parts. Presolvers: 6× faster than Gurobi and 19× than PaPILO (25× on the 69 common instances), leaving 68.4% of nonzeros against 61.7% and 66.7%. Inside the IPM: 48 against 37 solved and −40% SGM, with the failures of the no-presolve runs classified. External presolve: at most 21 solved with automatic re-annotation, about as many with the hand-built inherited annotation, slower end to end. Determinism costs 4.45 → 3.7 s; multi-node runs vary more than 2× on 14 of 71 instances; no significance tests (pp. 12–20, 26–27).
positioning: Places itself between the LP presolve literature (Andersen and Andersen 1995, Gondzio 1997, Achterberg et al. 2020) and structure-exploiting arrowhead solvers. Criticizes general-purpose libraries, including the group's own PaPILO, and measures PaPILO gaining only 1.25 from 1 to 64 threads on these LPs (compare S026's MIPLIB scaling). Gurobi is the reference for reduction strength. Extends S068 (pp. 3–4, 6, 11, 14).
writing: The abstract prints losses next to the speed-ups; three contributions; a 'Scope and limitations' paragraph before the results, with the hedge that carrying the results over to other AHLPs is not tested. Unreconciled numbers: the 64-process SGM appears as 4.39, 4.45 and 4.49 s; Gurobi presolves 82 of 82 instances but only 17 of the 18 large ones; 'do not make the IPM noticeably faster' against 124 → 118 s. A co-authored AI-use disclosure (pp. 1, 3, 13, 15, 17, 19, 26–27).
limits_future: Limits: energy models only; dependent on the modeller's annotation, which cannot yet be automated; two arrowhead-specific presolvers; no block-size balancing; little multi-node gain with large linking parts; dependencies through linking rows undetected; a reduction gap to Gurobi not explained by structure preservation. Future: make the presolve available to other structure-exploiting methods, add presolvers and tune, combine or overlap collectives (pp. 10, 13, 17, 20, 27).

title: A Numerically-safe Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for the Length-Constrained Cycle Partition Problem
contribution: A set-partitioning branch-price-and-cut for the length-constrained cycle partition problem. Its label-setting pricing exploits the undirected symmetry (one-direction bidirectional search), together with an ng-relaxation, symmetry breaking by critical time, triangle-inequality exploitation, and subset-row and clique cuts. Numerically safe dual bounds come from integer-scaled duals and exact integer pricing. It solves 51 of 84 benchmark instances (52 with cuts respected in pricing), with up to 76 nodes, against 37 (40 warm-started) for the SEC branch and cut on Gurobi. Safety costs about 40% extra time and never changed a certified bound.
problem_entry: Compact MTZ and SEC models of LCCP have weak relaxations and symmetry (solved up to 29 and 52 nodes); a set partitioning over cycles promises tight bounds, while floating-point column generation can return too-large bounds or miss columns (pp. 2–3, 13).
key_idea: Solve SP by branch-price-and-cut, with: label-setting pricing per start node (dominance, one-direction bidirectional merge, ng-relaxation with a Lagrangian bound, greedy pricing first); covering rows for nodes that satisfy the triangle inequality; SRC and clique cuts lifted to new columns; and safe bounds by scaling the duals to integers and pricing in exact integer arithmetic (pp. 4–17).
assumptions: Undirected graph, travel times ≥ 0 possibly non-metric, critical times > 0, duals free in sign, integral objective; pricing strongly NP-hard (Theorem 1); the 84-instance standard set of Hoppmann-Baum et al. 2022 ('14 to 100 nodes', though one instance has 124); how travel times are stored, and whether length feasibility is checked exactly, is not stated (pp. 3–4, 13, 17, 28).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: strong NP-hardness of pricing by reduction from Hamiltonian cycle with unit data (p. 4)
Feasibility pruning by induction over label extensions; Lemma 1 (dominance) via inclusion of extension sets and the monotone minimum critical time (pp. 5–6)
Theorem 2: completeness of one-direction bidirectional search with dominance, via the first forward label past the halfway point and transitivity of dominance (pp. 7–8)
Lemma 2: zero-dual nodes that satisfy the triangle inequality can be skipped, by a shortcut argument; covering-to-partitioning post-processing (pp. 9–10)
Lagrangian bound z*_MP ≥ z*_RMP + Σ_s min{0, z*_s}, valid under the ng-relaxation and rounded up by integrality; early branching (pp. 9, 16)

Dual repair, Algorithm 1: M = 10^15, π^int = ⌊M·π^inf⌋, exact integer check of dual feasibility over all RMP columns, M ← M/10 until feasible; cut duals and negative covering duals set to zero; pricing and bounds in integer arithmetic (pp. 13–14, 16)
Integrality argument: a safe bound changes a decision only when it crosses an integer boundary (pp. 13–14)
experiments: Setup: a Rust SCIP wrapper with parallel pricing (the rest of SCIP sequential) against the SEC branch and cut on Gurobi 13.0.1; 2 h limit, Xeon Gold 6338, exclusive nodes, 16 threads each; 84 instances; SGM (shift 1 s, timeouts at the limit) per table over the instances solved by any configuration listed there. Solved: 37 (bnc-sec), 46 (bnp-mcv, same start as bnc-sec), 51 (bnp-full), 40 (bnc-full, same best known start as bnp-full). Like-for-like factors 7.4× and 10.9×; the headline 14.7× comes from the unequal pair. Root gap 0.4% against 30.3%. One-at-a-time ablation with virtual best. Safety costs about 40% time, with no bound failures. Cuts separate on only 3 and 2 instances; SRCs respected in pricing give 52. Recount of Table 5: 15 instances solved only by bnp-full and 1 only by bnc-sec; Table 1's SGMs imply two instances solved only by bnc-full or bnp-mcv (inference). No seeds or significance tests (pp. 17–22, 25–28).
positioning: Reformulates the earlier LCCP models of co-author Mexi (Hoppmann et al. 2020; Hoppmann-Baum et al. 2022) with vehicle-routing and kidney-exchange machinery. The safe bounds follow Fukasawa and Poirrier 2017 and Baldacci et al. 2024, with Eifler and Gleixner 2023 and 2024 as background; the solver mismatch (SCIP against Gurobi) is argued to be conservative. As a problem-specific branch-price-and-cut by Gleixner's group, it does not fit SKILL.md's Roundtable contrast with Lübbecke (default branch and cut, [M17; LCCP26]) or the Honest Boundary (no decomposition research) (pp. 2–4, 12, 19).
writing: Worked examples on a 5-node instance; four numbered questions; light hedging. The headline denominators drift (14 previously unsolved, 14 more than bnc-sec, 52 against 40, while Table 5 gives 15), and the introduction's 14.7× uses the unequal pair. Slips: a 124-node instance against '14 to 100 nodes'; 11 cuts in one round against a limit of 10; 'same root bound quality' against root gaps of 1.9% and 0.2%; root gaps labelled 'average optimality gap'. Several typos (pp. 1–3, 8–9, 12–13, 17–23, 28).
limits_future: Limits: instances beyond 76 nodes unsolved and pricing dominates the time; the round-up property fails on t84 eil51; cuts rarely separate; heuristic dual bounds carry no guarantee; what happens when the dual repair fails is not described. Future: parallel or GPU-accelerated labeling, then a parallel tree search and more cuts once pricing is no longer the bottleneck (pp. 14, 19, 22–23).
